claims.text: Sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters can be formed on CeO2 nanorods.
The supported CoNiCuZnPd clusters are near-equiatomic and uniformly dispersed.
Repeated oxidative and reductive exposure induces reversible structural changes in the CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-nanorod clusters.
Oxidative conditions sacrificially oxidize the non-noble Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn components.
Oxidation produces Pd-containing nuclei encapsulated by non-noble-metal oxide shells.
The transient oxide layers are ultrathin.
The oxide shells inhibit diffusion of Pd atoms into CeO2.
The oxide layers protect the clusters against sintering.
The oxide layers prevent phase segregation and preserve chemical homogeneity.
Reduction following oxidation removes the oxide layers and restores the metallic cluster state and original morphology.
Oxidative NO exposure transforms the sub-nanometer clusters from a cuboctahedral form into a raft-like structure.
Cyclic modulation of atomic mobility sustains the active single-phase solid solution required for catalytic function.
Alternating oxidizing and H2 atmospheres is the controlled intervention, with an unchanging atmosphere as the control.
The relevant controlled temperature range is 773–1173 K.
Redox-cycled clusters will retain sub-nanometer size better than clusters held under a constant atmosphere.
Redox-cycled clusters will show reversible XANES or related spectroscopic changes.
Redox-cycled clusters will retain NO-reduction activity better than constant-atmosphere controls.
Constant oxidizing or constant reducing exposure will cause irreversible sintering or phase segregation and diminished catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism is limited to sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd clusters on CeO2 nanorods and may not apply to larger particles, other supports, or unsuitable cycling conditions.
Failure of cycling to produce a statistically significant improvement in size, single-phase structure, and activity relative to the constant-atmosphere control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes preservation of a single-phase solid solution, while the mechanism explicitly introduces a Pd@MOx core-shell state and a cuboctahedral-to-raft structural transformation. This is reconcilable only if 'preservation' refers to recovery after reduction rather than continuous single-phase retention during the oxidative portion of each cycle.
